customdata:
{"name": "Sun", "subtitle": "", "body": "Note: The Sun, our very own star, is a massive ball of hot plasma that sits at the center of our solar system.
It's the source of all life and energy on Earth, so I've colored it chlorophyll green in our plot!
* Type: A yellow dwarf star (G-type main-sequence star).
* Age: About 4.6 billion years old, and is expected to continue its current phase for about 5 billion years
more, then evolve into a Red Giant.
* Diameter: Roughly 1.4 million kilometers (865,000 miles), about 109 times the diameter of Earth.
* Mass: About 333,000 times the mass of Earth
* Composition: Primarily hydrogen (about 73%) and helium (about 25%), with trace amounts of other elements.
* Surface Temperature: 5778 K, around 5,500 degrees Celsius, or 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit
* Core Temperature: Around 15 million degrees Celsius (27 million degrees Fahrenheit)
* Stellar Class: Main-sequence. Stars in the prime of their lives, fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.
* Absolute Magnitude: 4.83
* Spectral Type: G2V
* Object Type: Star
The Sun is composed of several layers:
* Core: The innermost region where nuclear fusion occurs, converting hydrogen into helium and releasing energy.
* Radiative Zone: Energy from the core travels outward through this zone via radiation.
* Convective Zone: Energy is transported through this zone via convection (the movement of hot plasma).
* Photosphere: The visible surface of the Sun.
* Chromosphere: A thin layer above the photosphere.
* Corona: The outermost layer, a very hot and tenuous plasma that extends millions of kilometers into space.
Standard for comparison to other stars:
* Luminosity: 1.000000 Lsun
* Mass: 1.00 Msun
* Distance: 0 pc (0 ly)
* Plotting marker size: 12 px"}
data.name: Sun
text:
Sun
Note: The Sun, our very own star, is a massive ball of hot plasma that sits at the center of our solar system.
It's the source of all life and energy on Earth, so I've colored it chlorophyll green in our plot!
* Type: A yellow dwarf star (G-type main-sequence star).
* Age: About 4.6 billion years old, and is expected to continue its current phase for about 5 billion years
more, then evolve into a Red Giant.
* Diameter: Roughly 1.4 million kilometers (865,000 miles), about 109 times the diameter of Earth.
* Mass: About 333,000 times the mass of Earth
* Composition: Primarily hydrogen (about 73%) and helium (about 25%), with trace amounts of other elements.
* Surface Temperature: 5778 K, around 5,500 degrees Celsius, or 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit
* Core Temperature: Around 15 million degrees Celsius (27 million degrees Fahrenheit)
* Stellar Class: Main-sequence. Stars in the prime of their lives, fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.
* Absolute Magnitude: 4.83
* Spectral Type: G2V
* Object Type: Star
The Sun is composed of several layers:
* Core: The innermost region where nuclear fusion occurs, converting hydrogen into helium and releasing energy.
* Radiative Zone: Energy from the core travels outward through this zone via radiation.
* Convective Zone: Energy is transported through this zone via convection (the movement of hot plasma).
* Photosphere: The visible surface of the Sun.
* Chromosphere: A thin layer above the photosphere.
* Corona: The outermost layer, a very hot and tenuous plasma that extends millions of kilometers into space.
Standard for comparison to other stars:
* Luminosity: 1.000000 Lsun
* Mass: 1.00 Msun
* Distance: 0 pc (0 ly)
* Plotting marker size: 12 px

{"name": "New Horizons Jupiter Gravity Assist", "subtitle": "", "body": "Date: 2007-02-28 05:43:40 UTC
Distance: 0.01541 AU (2.31 million km)
Velocity relative to Jupiter: 21.22 km/s
Velocity relative to Sun: 23.00 km/s
Type: Gravity Assist

Fastest launch ever: 16.26 km/s Earth-relative,
combining with Earth's orbital velocity to ~43
km/s heliocentric (velocities add as vectors, not
scalars). The Sun's gravity steadily slowed it to
~19 km/s by Jupiter. The gravity assist added ~4
km/s, boosting speed to ~23 km/s -- partially
recovering what the Sun took. Without this boost,
Pluto arrival would have been three years later.

Source: NASA/JPL"}

_encyclopedia.Earth:
Horizons: 399. Our home planet, the third from the Sun.
* Earth-centered: do not select Earth; visualize shells at 0.02 AU.
* Heliocentric: select Earth with or without shells.
* Missions: Galileo, Cassini-Huygens, Rosetta, New Horizons, JUNO, Parker Solar Probe, Deep Impact, NEAR Shoemaker, Solar Orbiter.
_encyclopedia.Arrokoth:
Horizons: 2014 MU69. Arrokoth is the most distant object ever visited by a spacecraft, New Horizons, on January 1, 2019.
  * Official Name: Arrokoth (formerly known as Ultima Thule)
  * JPL Horizons Designation: (486958) 2014 MU69
  * Location: Kuiper Belt, a region beyond Neptune populated by icy bodies
  * Discovered: 2014 by the New Horizons team using the Hubble Space Telescope
  * Shape: A contact binary, meaning it's made of two lobes joined together. It resembles a flattened snowman.
  * Size: About 36 km (22 miles) long at its longest axis.
  * Color: Very red, even redder than Pluto. This is due to the presence of complex organic molecules called tholins, formed by radiation interacting with ices.
  * Surface: Smooth with few craters, suggesting it's ancient and hasn't experienced many impacts.
  * Composition: Likely a mix of ices (water, methane, etc.) and organic materials.
  * Significance:
    * Most Distant Object Explored: Arrokoth is the most distant and most primitive object ever visited by a spacecraft.
    * Clues to Solar System Formation: Because it's so far from the Sun, Arrokoth has likely remained relatively unchanged since the early days of the solar system. Studying it helps us understand the conditions and processes that led to the formation of planets and other celestial bodies.
    * Building Blocks of Life: Recent research suggests that Arrokoth may contain sugars like ribose and glucose, which are essential for life as we know it. This raises exciting questions about the potential for life to exist elsewhere in the universe.
    * New Horizons Flyby on January 1, 2019 (See "New Horizons" for more information):
      * Plot Arrokoth as the center body, and New Horizons, to visualize.
      * Closest approach by New Horizons on January 1, 2019, at 3537.7 km, at 5:34:31 UTC.
      * Detailed Images: Stunning images revealed Arrokoth's unique shape and surface features.
      * Compositional Data: Instruments on New Horizons analyzed the light reflected from Arrokoth, giving us information about its composition.
      * Insights into Formation: Scientists are using the data to create models of how Arrokoth formed, which has implications for our understanding of planet formation in general.
_encyclopedia.Pluto:
Horizons: 999. Dwarf planet in a TRUE BINARY system with Charon.

ORBITAL RESONANCE:
* Pluto is a PLUTINO - locked in 3:2 resonance with Neptune.
* Makes 2 orbits for every 3 of Neptune's (period: 248 years).
* Currently moving toward aphelion (49 AU, ~2114).
* Perihelion was 1989 (30 AU - closer than Neptune!).
* ANTI-PLUTO: Orcus is in the SAME resonance but 180 deg out of phase!
   When Pluto is at perihelion, Orcus is at aphelion, and vice versa.

THREE VIEW MODES:
* Heliocentric (Sun-centered): Select Pluto to see its orbit around the Sun.
* Pluto-centered: Do NOT select Pluto; shows moons orbiting Pluto.
   Like geocentric view - convenient but hides real mechanics.
* Barycenter-centered: Select "Pluto-Charon Barycenter" as center.
  and select Pluto and its moons to see TRUE orbits.
   * Shows TRUE orbital mechanics - both Pluto AND Charon orbit in a dance
     around their common center of mass (barycenter)! This is why Pluto-Charon is
     called a binary planet: the barycenter is OUTSIDE Pluto.

BINARY PLANET PHYSICS:
* Mass ratio: Charon/Pluto = 12%
* Barycenter: 2,035 km from Pluto's center (outside its 1,188 km radius!)
* Pluto orbits barycenter: ~2,100 km radius
* Charon orbits barycenter: ~17,500 km radius (same period: 6.387 days)
* Compare: Earth-Moon barycenter is inside Earth - not a true binary.

Missions: New Horizons (2015 flyby); Pluto Orbiter concept under study.

HTML: ~22 MB per frame with all shells/moons.

***SET MANUAL SCALE TO 0.0003 AU TO PLOT NEW HORIZONS-ARROKOTH FLYBY ON 2019-1-1.

Horizons: -98. New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015, now exploring the Kuiper Belt.
* The New Horizons space probe is an interplanetary space probe built by the Applied Physics Laboratory of Johns Hopkins
University for NASA.
* It was launched on January 19, 2006 with the primary mission to conduct a flyby study of Pluto and its moons in the Kuiper Belt. It is the first spacecraft to explore Pluto and the Kuiper Belt up close.
* Approaches 2002 JF56 on June 13, 2006 to within 102,000 km at 10:06 UTC
* Jupiter gravity assist on February 28, 2007, 05:43 UTC, 2.3045(10)^6 km
* Pluto Flyby: On July 14, 2015, Pluto-Charon encounter at 11:49:57 UTC. New Horizons made its historic closest approach to Pluto, capturing stunning images and valuable scientific data about the dwarf planet and its moons.
* Kuiper Belt Exploration: After its Pluto encounter, New Horizons continued its journey into the Kuiper Belt.
* Arrokoth (2014 MU69) flyby on January 1, 2019, at 3537.7 km, at 5:34:31 UTC.
* Scientific Instruments: New Horizons carries a suite of scientific instruments, including cameras, spectrometers, and plasma analyzers, to study the composition, atmosphere, and environment of Pluto and other Kuiper Belt objects.
* Continuing Mission: New Horizons is still traveling through the Kuiper Belt, and NASA may extend its mission to explore other distant objects in the future.
_encyclopedia.Sun:
Horizons: 10. The star at the center of our solar system. To display structure and atmosphere select "Solar Shells".

* Missions:
  * Pioneer 5 (NASA/DOD, 1960): Measured magnetic field phenomena, solar flare particles, and ionization.
  * Helios 1 & 2 (DFVLR/NASA, 1974 & 1976): Studied solar wind, magnetic and electric fields, cosmic rays, and dust.
  * ISEE-3 (NASA, 1978): Observed solar phenomena in conjunction with Earth-orbiting satellites, comets.
  * Ulysses (ESA/NASA, 1990-2009): Observed the Sun's polar regions and the solar wind at high solar latitudes.
  * WIND (NASA, 1994-Present): Still active, it provides continuous measurements of the solar wind.
  * SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) (ESA/NASA, 1995-Present): A continuous view from its core to the solar wind.
  * ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer) (NASA, 1997-Present): Measures particles from the solar wind and galactic cosmic rays.
  * Hinode (JAXA/NASA/ESA/STFC, 2006-Present): Explores the Sun's magnetic fields.
  * STEREO (Solar TErrestrial RElations Observatory) (NASA, 2006-Present): Imaging the 3D structure of coronal mass ejections.
  * Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) (NASA, 2010-Present): High-resolution images of solar flares and eruptions.
  * IRIS (Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph) (NASA, 2013-Present): Sun's lower atmosphere (chromosphere and transition).
  * Parker Solar Probe (NASA, 2018-Present): Flew through the corona to study coronal heating and solar wind acceleration.
  * Solar Orbiter (ESA/NASA, 2020-Present): Provides unprecedented insight into how our local star "works" with 10 science instruments.
  * PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) (NASA, Launched March 2025): Will study the Sun's outer atmosphere.
  * Solar Polar Orbit Observatory (Planned 2029): Will study views of its polar regions.

* Missions: Pioneer 10 and 11; Voyager 1 and 2; Ulysses; Cassini-Huygens; New Horizons; Galileo;
